analysis.one_liner: Removes the requirement that federal construction contractors pay locally prevailing wages.
analysis.headline: The bill to repeal the Davis-Bacon Act never received a hearing or vote in the Senate labor committee and died when the 116th Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: The Davis-Bacon Act requires companies working on federally funded construction projects to pay workers the locally prevailing wage — essentially the local market rate for each trade, which on most federal jobs means union-scale pay. This bill would repeal that requirement entirely, letting contractors on federal projects pay whatever wages they choose. It was introduced by Sen. Mike Lee and referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, which never acted on it.
analysis.who_benefits: Construction contractors who win federal projects, especially nonunion open-shop firms that could bid lower by paying less than prevailing wage. Federal, state, and local governments (and taxpayers) would see some savings on construction contracts because bids would be lower.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals subchapter IV of chapter 31 of title 40, which contains the Davis-Bacon prevailing wage requirement for federally financed construction, alteration, and repair work [S3].
Nullifies any reference in any other law to the Davis-Bacon wage requirement, removing the standard from federal contracting rules across the board [S3].
Takes effect 30 days after enactment but leaves existing contracts and contracts from already-outstanding bid solicitations untouched [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Construction workers on federally funded projects, who would lose the prevailing-wage floor that guarantees local market or union-scale pay; organized labor would lose its strongest wage standard on public work.

drawbacks.text: Workers building public buildings and public works would lose the wage floor that ties their pay to local prevailing rates for each trade, effectively cutting pay on federally funded jobs [S2].

Supporters of prevailing wage rules argue the standard helps ensure trained, quality workmanship and stable local hiring on public projects; repeal would remove that protection while also removing the compliance paperwork contractors cite as a cost.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would lower the cost of federal construction contracts for taxpayers, and its supporters point to that plus reduced paperwork as the gain. The cost falls directly on the workers doing that construction, who lose the guarantee of local prevailing wages. Since the savings come from paying workers less, the bill is essentially a transfer from federal construction labor to contractors and government buyers.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate labor committee, which never scheduled a hearing or vote, and it expired when the 116th Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Sen. Mike Lee introduced the Davis-Bacon Repeal Act in the Senate on October 17, 2019 [S1].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee on the day of introduction [S5].
The committee took no further action on the bill, and it never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote before the Congress ended [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Construction workers and the building trades are better off because the bill died: the prevailing-wage floor on federally funded construction stays in place, and contractors continue to bear the higher labor costs it requires.

for.name: Sen. Mike Lee
for.role: U.S. Senator from Utah and bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to repeal the Davis-Bacon prevailing wage requirement

for.name: 8 Senate Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the repeal bill, adding it to the roll of sponsors

sides.party_line_note: All sponsors and cosponsors were Republicans (the sponsor plus 8 cosponsors, all R), and no Democrat sponsored or cosponsored the bill; with Republicans holding the Senate and the chairmanship of the labor committee at the time, the lack of action was not a floor defeat but a lack of committee movement [S4][S5].

industries.note: Repeal would let contractors on federally funded jobs pay below prevailing wage, lowering their labor costs and bids — savings that come directly out of construction workers' pay.
Davis-Bacon is the strongest wage standard protecting union-scale pay on public construction; the bill would eliminate it, undercutting union contractors' ability to compete against lower-wage bids.
These firms gain the most from repeal, since prevailing-wage rules are what prevent them from underbidding union-scale work on federal projects with lower payrolls.
